title: Prefill handoff with attention-lane allocator and kernel prober
creator: Diego Morales
description: Problem: We observe sporadic 95th/99th token latency spikes when long prefill requests are admitted alongside many short decode-only requests. Root cause analysis shows cross-interference at two points: (1) prefill->decode handoff causes fragmentation of kernel execution slots, and (2) attention-heavy long sequences push kernel selection toward slower attention kernels for mixed workloads. Goal: reduce tail latency by introducing an explicit prefill handoff window and an attention-lane allocator that groups requests by attention cost and kernel probe score. This ticket implements the runtime changes, the admission handshake, and the experiment harness for rollout.
acceptance_criteria: 95th token latency reduced by >=20% for mixed prefill+decode workloads on our staging cluster compared to baseline
No throughput regression (>3%) for steady-state decode-only workloads after enabling feature
Fallback correctness: if kernel prober cannot find an optimized kernel in 25ms, request falls back to current default path with no correctness deviation
Feature gated behind runtime flag and rollout can be toggled per-tenant via console
technical_design: Introduce a lightweight prefill handoff token: when a prefill finishes, runtime emits a handoff record with request metadata (sequence_length, attention_sparsity_hint, estimated_kv_size) into the per-GPU handoff queue

Attention-lane allocator: categorize incoming requests into 3 lanes (low-attention, medium-attention, high-attention) using a fast heuristic (first-8-tokens attention variance + model-provided hint header). Lanes are used to influence admission windows and batch shaping.

Kernel prober: background probe that attempts small synthetic prefills for representative shapes to measure per-kernel latency for current GPU and quantization profile. Results cached with TTL and exposed to admission logic.
Prefill handoff window: allow a short prioritized reservation (configurable ms) for a kernel handoff to drain KV and schedule decode kernels contiguous to prefill to reduce fragmentation.
Admission changes: add lane-aware admission quotas that limit how many high-attention prefill requests can be admitted concurrently to avoid pushing most batches into expensive kernel choices.
Metrics and tracing: add handoff lifecycle spans, lane tags, kernel-prober scores, and prefill->decode contiguous scheduling ratio.
Safety: fall back to legacy admission when configuration invalid or probe metrics stale. All new paths behind runtime flag 'prefill_handoff_v1'.
rollout_plan: Feature behind runtime flag and per-tenant gate in console
Stage 1 (canary): enable for internal tenant + 2 low-traffic customers, collect metrics for 48 hours
Stage 2 (staged rollout): enable for 20% of tenants with medium traffic + enforce stricter logging, run A/B for 7 days
Stage 3 (gradual): ramp to 100% if metrics show no regressions and tail latency improves
Kill-switch: immediate disable via console and automatic rollback if error-rate or latency delta exceeds thresholds
testing_plan: Unit tests for allocator heuristics and handoff queue correctness
Integration tests on local GPU cluster simulating mixed trace (mix of long-chat prefill requests and short decode-only requests)
Chaos test: inject slow kernel responses and ensure fallbacks trigger and maintain correctness
Performance test: run multi-tenant load test in staging with kernel prober enabled and collect 50/95/99 latency distributions
Canary dashboards: runtime token-level latency, handoff-success-rate, kernel-prober hit-rate, and lane admission ratios
notes: Design review held 2026-03-11: feedback to reduce probe frequency to avoid extra GPU work; we adjust TTL to 10s and sample only when GPU utilization < 70%
PM asked to add a per-customer opt-out; implemented via existing tenant flags in console
Implementation split: allocator + admission in runtime core (Ayesha), kernel prober as separate background service (Ben Chen), handoff tracing (SRE)
Related research: look at attention-sparsity hints from model opt-in (cf. model-ops format) for better lane classification
